newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax plan seen boosting shares but not Bunds.
newsitem.headline: German tax plan seen boosting shares but not Bunds.

text.p: German shares will generally benefit from an estimated 10 billion mark cut in corporate taxes contained in a wide-ranging tax reform plan, German market strategists said on Thursday.
But German Bunds were likely to show their usual disdain for domestic news, as investors continued to focus on more international issues.
While equities stand to gain from the tax reform, share analysts said Bonn might still have some tricks up its sleeve that could offset the benefits from lower corporate tax.

"We do not yet completely know what measures Bonn plans to counter-balance all of this. But it seems clear that companies will have to make their contribution -- that is the real question now," Manfred Link, strategist at DB Research said.

Under the reform proposals, which still have to passed by parliament, corporate taxes will fall in two stages to 35 percent for retained profits and to 25 percent for profits distributed to shareholders.
The move would shave an estimated 9.8 billion marks ($6 billion) off the national corporate tax bill.

Link said, however, that there had already been speculation that if Bonn sought to claw back some of that tax reduction -- for example through an increase in work-related contributions -- employers were likely to have to pay the lion's share.

The proposals, released early in the morning, barely made an impression on the German DAX-30 index of top shares, which was determined to take a breather after recent climbs to record-levels. It closed 4.79 points up at 3,033.46.
Dealers said the market had been widely banking on a net cut in corporate taxes and had already priced the impact in.

Moreover, the increasing proportion of business that German companies were doing abroad -- and was thus subject to other tax systems -- meant the overall benefit would be watered down for the most international firms.

"It could well be that it is the small and medium stocks, which don't do as much of their business abroad, that stand to benefit most," said Rod Hinkel, German strategist at London-based Banque Paribas Capital Markets.
There was, however, little concern that an accompanying tax clamp-down on profits from speculative share transactions would worry the largest investors.
"Most of the market players are professionals who are investing long-term anyway," said Michael Bock, head of German equities at the Frankfurt office of investment house BZW.
The new proposals will mean that investors will have to hold on to a share for a year before they can sell it at a tax-free profit, compared with the current six months.

German debt, which was traded largely flat as the market digested money supply data and the implications of a Bundesbank decision to keep interest rates unchanged, was not seen benefiting from the reform.

"The market has so many other potentially more important issues to deal with, like the currency union, that this situation has not had a very big impact," said Florian Staerk, bond analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel Bank.
In the longer term a real tax reform would rather be bearish for the bond market as it could promote economic growth, the very thing that causes bonds to be sold, he said.
